title: How to Disagree Without Losing the Relationship
excerpt: We are losing friendships over arguments at a rate our parents would not recognize. Here is how to hold your convictions and keep your people.
body:
We live in a moment that has trained us to treat disagreement as a reason to end a relationship. Unfriend, unfollow, cut off, walk away. The wider culture has taught us that loving people requires agreeing with them and that those who differ are not merely wrong but dangerous. Christians have caught the same disease, and it is killing our witness, because a faith that cannot stay in the room with people who disagree has nothing to offer a divided world.

Jesus kept company with people across every line that mattered in his day. Zealots who wanted Rome overthrown and tax collectors who collaborated with Rome sat at the same table as his disciples. He did not require them to agree before he loved them. He loved them into a room together. That is the model, and it is harder than picking a side.

## Decide the relationship outranks the argument

The first move is a decision made before the conversation: this person matters more to me than winning this point. If you have not settled that in advance, the heat of the moment will settle it for you, and you will choose the win and lose the person. Most arguments are not actually about the topic. They are about whether each person feels respected. Decide they will leave the conversation feeling respected even if neither of you moved, and you have already kept the relationship.

## Seek to understand before you answer

Proverbs says that to answer before listening is folly and shame. Most of our disagreements are folly and shame by that definition, because we are loading our rebuttal while the other person is still talking. Try instead to state their view back to them so well that they say yes, that is what I mean. This costs your pride, because it means genuinely hearing a position you find wrong. But the person who feels truly understood can tolerate disagreement. The person who feels caricatured cannot.

## Stay curious about the why

Underneath most positions is a fear or a wound or a value worth honoring. The person whose politics alarm you is often protecting something they love. Ask why they hold what they hold, and listen for the thing underneath. You may still disagree with their conclusion, but you will understand the human being who reached it, and understanding is the soil where relationship survives disagreement. Contempt grows where curiosity has died.

## Refuse contempt even when you keep conviction

You can hold a conviction firmly and refuse contempt entirely. These are different things, though the culture treats them as one. To disagree is to think someone is wrong. To hold them in contempt is to think they are beneath you. The first is honest. The second is poison, and people feel it through every polite word. I have caught contempt in my own voice while saying all the right things, and the contempt is what the other person heard, not the rightness. Repent of the contempt and the disagreement can stay.

## Know what is worth the cost

Not everything is worth a hard conversation, and not every relationship survives every disagreement. There are convictions you cannot trade away, and there are people who will leave no matter how gently you hold your ground. Wisdom is knowing which hills are worth standing on and which arguments are just your pride looking for a fight. Most of the arguments we lose relationships over are the second kind. Save your stand for the things that actually warrant it, and let the rest go.

## Be the safe person in a hostile time

In a culture sorting itself into camps that no longer speak, the Christian who can hold deep convictions and still love across the line is a rare and powerful witness. You become the safe person, the one a friend can disagree with and not lose. That safety is its own testimony to a gospel that reconciles enemies. The world is full of people who will affirm you only if you agree. Be the one who loves them whether or not they do.

## This week

Think of one relationship currently strained by a disagreement, and take a step toward the person that has nothing to do with the argument. A call, a meal, a kind word that says you matter more to me than this. If the topic comes up, practice stating their view back until they agree you have understood it, before you say a single word in reply. You will be surprised how much heat drains out of a disagreement when the other person finally feels heard.
